title: Ethical use of ChatGPT in education—Best practices to combat AI-induced plagiarism
extended_summary:
This opinion paper addresses the growing concern that generative AI tools such as ChatGPT can facilitate plagiarism and undermine academic integrity in education. Rather than reporting an empirical experiment, it synthesizes risks, ethical issues, and practical considerations around student use of large language models and argues that educators and institutions need proactive strategies to respond.

The paper surveys a range of anti-plagiarism and assessment-design approaches, including AI-usage policies, plagiarism-detection tools, adaptive testing, reflective writing, peer assessment, oral examinations, personalized tasks, multimodal assessments, and ongoing low-stakes monitoring. It also discusses the limitations of technical detection, including false positives, privacy concerns, resource demands, and the need for continual updates as AI systems evolve.

The context is general education and higher education, with attention to teachers, institutions, and students rather than a specific sample or intervention trial. The main conclusion is that the most effective response is a blended approach combining ethics education, thoughtful assessment redesign, and technological detection, supported by institutional policy and ongoing teacher training to promote responsible AI use while preserving academic integrity.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed opinion/article rather than an empirical study. It offers conceptual guidance and literature-informed recommendations but no primary design, comparison group, or measurable intervention effect estimates.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has potentially broad practical relevance for K-12 and higher education assessment policy, but it does not demonstrate measured impact. Its likely impact is modest and indirect because it mainly proposes strategies rather than evaluating outcomes.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT as a generative AI writing and response tool in education, discussed as a student-facing system that can generate essays, assignment answers, and other academic text that may be used ethically or misused for plagiarism.
Learning analytics used to track learner progress and detect unexplained performance patterns that may indicate AI-enabled plagiarism.
AI-detection and plagiarism-detection tools used to flag suspicious student submissions and support instructor review rather than provide instructional tutoring.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can support writing and communication but also substantially increases the risk of AI-assisted plagiarism in essays and other written assignments. It does not report new empirical writing-performance data; instead, it synthesizes prior work and practitioner observations about generated text quality, false citations, and difficulty distinguishing AI-written from student-written text.
finding.measure: Quality and originality of student written assignments; plagiarism/AI-detection indicators

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims generative AI can be used to stimulate creativity, critical thinking, and problem solving when paired with personalized, reflective, oral, and project-based assessments. However, this is a narrative claim rather than a directly estimated effect; no sample size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, creativity, problem solving, and authenticity of student demonstrations

finding.finding_summary: The paper asserts that AI-detection tools, adaptive testing, learning analytics, and modular assessment design can help instructors identify suspicious work earlier and reduce plagiarism-related workload over time. This is presented as a conceptual benefit with no primary data or effect estimate reported.
finding.measure: Instructor workload, speed of plagiarism detection, and assessment monitoring efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main contribution is a set of institutional best-practice recommendations for policies, assessment redesign, AI-use guidelines, awareness campaigns, and detection systems to manage generative AI ethically. The discussion is qualitative/opinion-based and does not provide a causal estimate, but it strongly argues these measures improve academic integrity governance.
finding.measure: Institutional policy, governance, and academic integrity practices
